nodes.label: Detoxifying wild foods
nodes.desc: Grating, soaking, leaching, fermenting and cooking in the right order made poisonous staples safe, with no idea of cyanide or tannin. Found by trial and kept by copying the successful: Henrich's model case of adaptation without understanding. Date rough.

nodes.label: Nixtamalisation of maize
nodes.desc: Cooking maize in lime or ash water releases niacin, making maize a sufficient staple (roughly 1500 to 1200 BC, rough). Europe took maize without the method and got pellagra among the poor (Casal, Asturias 1735, memory): know-how travelled less well than the crop.

nodes.label: Collective brain (skill pool)
nodes.desc: A complex skill lasts only while enough connected people practise it and learners copy the best. Kline and Boyd (2010): island population predicts fishing toolkit size and complexity across ten Oceanic societies (checked). Contested by Vaesen et al. (2016).

nodes.label: Tasmanian loss of skills
nodes.desc: Cut off by rising seas, Tasmania had about 24 tool types at contact (checked): no hafted or bone tools, no fish taken. Henrich reads it as loss in a small population (contested). Depth of know-how is lost faster than it is built.

nodes.label: Written craft recipes
nodes.place: Nineveh (Assyrian glass texts); later Theophilus, about 1120
nodes.desc: Steps for batches and furnaces written down with rites alongside, and little theory (memory). The first form in which craft know-how left the hand: recipes without reasons.

nodes.label: Printed craft manuals
nodes.desc: Mining, smelting, assay and glass put into print as methods (memory); books of secrets ran to dozens of editions. Print lowered the cost of reaching know-how that guilds held close.

nodes.label: Encyclopedie plates of trades
nodes.desc: Diderot and d'Alembert's Encyclopedie (1751 to 1772) with eleven volumes of plates of trades (memory): craft methods opened to any literate reader. A key cut in Mokyr's access costs.

nodes.label: Hereditary crafts and castes
nodes.desc: Know-how passed parent to child within lineages or endogamous groups: cheap to transmit, narrow in reach, inherited like land. Even medieval masters were often masters' sons (part 05).

nodes.label: Craft secrecy as property
nodes.desc: Venice moved its glass furnaces to Murano in 1291 and forbade glassmakers to emigrate (memory). A secret earns a monopoly rent but risks loss with its holders; most 1851 exhibits were protected by secrecy, not patents (part 07).

nodes.label: Murano glass monopoly
nodes.desc: Venice's island glass industry, held by secrecy and emigration bans, made the clearest glass of its day. Its fugitive workers spread facon de Venise glass across Europe in the 16th and 17th centuries (memory).

nodes.label: Venetian cristallo glass
nodes.desc: Nearly colourless soda glass from purified Levantine plant ash and selected sand, credited to Angelo Barovier about 1450 (memory). Clear glass was the precondition for lenses and fine instruments.

nodes.label: Meissen hard-paste porcelain
nodes.desc: Bottger and Tschirnhaus found a hard-paste body about 1708; the works opened 1710 under oath-bound arcanists, who later defected (memory). Import substitution of Chinese porcelain after centuries of failed copying.

nodes.label: Chamberlen forceps secret
nodes.desc: The obstetric forceps kept as a family secret for over a century and published in the 1730s (memory): know-how held as household property.

nodes.label: Machine espionage (Lombe, Slater)
nodes.place: Piedmont to Derby; Britain to Rhode Island
nodes.desc: John Lombe drew Italian silk-throwing machines (1716 to 1717) for the Derby silk mill, about 1721 (memory); Slater carried Arkwright's system in his head in 1789 (part 07). Tacit know-how moved with people despite export bans.

nodes.label: Lombe's Derby silk mill
nodes.desc: Water-powered silk throwing on copied Italian machines, protected by Thomas Lombe's 1718 patent; often called England's first factory (memory).

nodes.label: Journeymen's travels
nodes.desc: Journeymen moved between masters and towns (Wanderjahre), carrying methods; Epstein argued this was the main channel of technical diffusion (contested, Ogilvie). The masterpiece certified the skill before mastership.

nodes.label: Balance and standard weights
nodes.desc: An equal-arm beam judged against weights kept to a standard by an authority (rough date). The basis of silver by weight, fair trade and assay; Lavoisier's mass balance (1789) rested on a better one.

nodes.label: Steelyard
nodes.desc: A beam with one sliding weight for quick weighing of bulk goods at markets and customs (memory).

nodes.label: Touchstone assay
nodes.desc: A gold streak on a black stone compared with streaks of touch-needles of known alloy: quick, cheap, nearly non-destructive, good to a few parts in a hundred (rough). The check behind gold coin and plate.

nodes.label: Fire assay and mint trial
nodes.desc: Cupel and assay balance give silver or gold content to a part in a thousand (rough); England tested its coin publicly from 1282 (memory). Let mints be audited and ores be valued before purchase.

nodes.label: Calendar marks and gnomon
nodes.desc: Solstice alignments (Newgrange about 3200 BC, memory), heliacal risings and the gnomon's noon shadow read the year. Guo Shoujing's 40-foot gnomon (1276 to 1279) fixed the tropical year closely (memory). Local sowing windows stayed lore.

nodes.label: Measuring rods and survey chains
nodes.desc: A master length held by an authority, copied as rods and ropes; Gunter's 66-foot chain (1620, memory) made the acre ten square chains. Fields, cadastres, rent and tax by area depend on it.

nodes.label: Triangulation and national surveys
nodes.desc: Angles measured with divided instruments from a base line give whole countries' maps (memory). State science before laboratories.

nodes.label: Water clocks
nodes.desc: Regulated flow measured hours, including at night, for temples and courts (memory). Su Song's tower at Kaifeng (1092) drove an armillary sphere through a water-wheel escapement (memory).

nodes.label: Su Song's astronomical clock
nodes.desc: A water-driven clock tower with an escapement, finished 1092 (memory); not continued after the city fell. A Song technique on a narrow base.

nodes.label: Mechanical clock (verge and foliot)
nodes.desc: Weight-driven iron wheels regulated by a verge escapement, first for monastic hours and cathedrals, then town towers from the mid-14th century (memory). Clockmakers became a school of gear-cutting that fed machine building.

nodes.label: Public clock time and work hours
nodes.desc: Town clocks and work bells set equal hours and wages by time (Landes, Thompson; memory); the long tightening of time discipline ran into the factory day.

nodes.label: Pendulum clock
nodes.desc: Huygens's clocks erred under a minute a day, later under ten seconds (checked); the anchor escapement (about 1670) and balance spring (1675) followed. Precision timekeeping for astronomy and as a standard.

nodes.label: Magnetic compass
nodes.desc: A magnetised steel needle shows north in any weather: described by Shen Kuo 1088, used at sea by about 1100, in Europe by about 1190 (memory). Needs lodestone and good steel.

nodes.label: Portolan charts and rutters
nodes.desc: Charts drawn from compass bearings and pilots' records (about 1275, memory); rutters wrote down the local facts of soundings, landmarks and tides.

nodes.label: Astrolabe, quadrant and octant
nodes.desc: Brass instruments with divided scales read a star's altitude for latitude and time; perfected in the Islamic world, mariner's astrolabe in the 1480s, Hadley's octant 1731 (memory).

nodes.label: Marine chronometer
nodes.desc: A spring timekeeper holding home-port time gives longitude. Harrison's H4 lost about 5 seconds in 81 days to Jamaica, 1761 to 1762 (checked). Cheap only in the 19th century.

nodes.label: Longitude prize
nodes.desc: Parliament offered up to 20,000 pounds for longitude at sea to half a degree (checked). Harrison got about 8,750 pounds by petition in 1773 (checked); the Board paid many smaller awards and funded the Nautical Almanac (1767, memory).

nodes.label: Spectacles and the lens trade
nodes.desc: Ground convex lenses for reading, about 1286 (checked); organised manufacture in Venice by 1300 to 1301 (checked); cheap pedlar goods by the 16th century. Longer working sight for scribes and fine craftsmen (Landes, contested).

nodes.label: Telescope
nodes.desc: Two spectacle lenses in a tube; Lipperhey's patent petition (2 October 1608) was refused as too easy to copy, and he was paid 300 guilders for an instrument (checked). Galileo saw Jupiter's moons in 1610.

nodes.label: Microscope
nodes.desc: Compound microscopes from the 1620s; Leeuwenhoek's single lenses about 270 times showed animalcules in 1676 (memory). Microbes were seen two centuries before they were tied to disease.

nodes.label: Lead crystal glass
nodes.desc: Dense, brilliant lead glass from coal-fired furnaces (memory); its dispersion let Dollond pair crown and flint glass in achromatic lenses (1758, memory).

nodes.label: Optical glass industry
nodes.desc: Stirred, homogeneous glasses designed for optics (memory). Its line runs to Zeiss, sole maker of the optics for ASML's EUV machines (part 13).

nodes.label: Barometer and air pump
nodes.desc: A mercury column showed air has weight (1643); Pascal 1648; Guericke's and Boyle's pumps in the 1650s (memory). The epistemic base of the atmospheric engine, in Mokyr's reading (contested).

nodes.label: Mercury thermometer
nodes.desc: Galileo's thermoscope about 1593 became a measuring instrument with even-bore tubes, mercury (1714) and fixed scales (Fahrenheit 1724, Celsius 1742) (memory). Brewers and dyers worked by degrees.

nodes.label: Alembic and glass still
nodes.desc: Glass and copper stills refined in the Islamic world separate the volatile part of a substance (memory). The chemist's bench: perfume, spirits, mineral acids.

nodes.label: Distilled spirits
nodes.desc: Aqua vitae distilled from wine (12th century, memory): a medical then a drinking trade; later taxed by strength measured with a hydrometer.

nodes.label: Aqua fortis parting of gold
nodes.desc: Nitric acid from the still dissolves silver from gold (about 1300, memory), joining assay and refining to glassware.

nodes.label: Thermometer and saccharometer in brewing
nodes.desc: Mash heat by thermometer and malt bought by measured extract (memory): an old craft moved onto instruments, then into laboratories.

nodes.label: Carlsberg Laboratory
nodes.desc: A brewer's research laboratory: Hansen's pure yeast culture (1883) and Sorensen's pH scale (1909) (memory). Industrial research began in old food trades as well as new chemistry.

nodes.label: Borosilicate laboratory glass
nodes.desc: Heat- and acid-resistant glass for apparatus (memory); the research laboratory is built of it.

nodes.label: Dividing engine
nodes.desc: Machine division of instrument scales; the Board of Longitude paid Ramsden to publish it (memory), so accurate sextants could be made in quantity. Precision makes precision.

nodes.label: London instrument makers
nodes.desc: Brass, glass and divided-scale makers exporting across Europe (rough); their workshops trained mechanics. Watt was Glasgow University's instrument maker.

nodes.label: Gauges, gauge blocks and standards labs
nodes.place: US armouries; Paris (metre 1799); Berlin PTR 1887; NPL 1900; NBS 1901
nodes.desc: Go and no-go gauges at the US armouries, Johansson's gauge blocks (1896) and national standards laboratories made units a public good (memory). Electrical units needed them before power could be sold.

nodes.label: Babylonian astronomical diaries
nodes.desc: Nightly records of sky, weather, river levels and prices from about 652 BC to the first century BC (memory): the longest run of ancient observations, from which period relations were found.

nodes.label: Manorial account rolls
nodes.desc: Reeves' yearly accounts of seed, yield, prices and wages; Winchester's pipe rolls survive from 1208 (memory). A control instrument whose long run is now the evidence for medieval yields.

nodes.label: Husbandry treatises
nodes.desc: Advice on oxen and horses, seed rates and checking reeves (memory): the first farm-management books, leaning on the accounts.

nodes.label: Parish registers
nodes.desc: Baptisms, marriages and burials recorded by order from 1538 (memory): the source of historical demography.

nodes.label: Bills of mortality
nodes.desc: Weekly counts of burials by cause from the parish clerks, begun 1592, resumed 1603, printed every Thursday (checked).

nodes.label: Graunt's political arithmetic
nodes.desc: Graunt read seventy years of bills (1662): sex ratios, seasons, plague years; London about 384,000 people against guesses of two million (checked). Petty named the method.

nodes.label: Life tables
nodes.desc: Halley's table from Breslau's records priced annuities (1693, memory); the Equitable (1762) priced life policies by age (memory).

nodes.label: Civil registration of deaths
nodes.place: England and Wales (General Register Office; Farr)
nodes.desc: Deaths registered with cause, organised by William Farr from 1839 (memory). Snow's 1854 comparison used it: 315 cholera deaths per 10,000 houses on the downstream company against 37 on Lambeth's (checked).

nodes.label: Controlled comparison trials
nodes.desc: Lind gave twelve scurvy patients six treatments in pairs; citrus cured (memory). The navy issued lemon juice generally only in 1795.

nodes.label: Rothamsted field trials
nodes.desc: Lawes and Gilbert's plots from 1843; Broadbalk wheat is the oldest continuing field experiment (checked). Settled the nitrogen question against Liebig (memory) while Lawes sold superphosphate.

nodes.label: Statistics of experiments
nodes.desc: The t-test for small brewery samples (1908, memory); Fisher hired at Rothamsted in 1919 built replication, blocking and analysis of variance (checked), and randomisation. The basis of randomised trials.

nodes.label: Agricultural experiment stations
nodes.desc: State-funded farm research (memory), tied in the US to land-grant colleges; the route by which hybrid maize came out of public research.

nodes.label: Bakewell's progeny-tested breeding
nodes.desc: Close breeding and letting rams to judge them by their offspring (memory). New Leicester sheep fattened fast; the method was the point.

nodes.label: Stud and herd books
nodes.place: England (General Stud Book 1791; Coates's Herd Book 1822)
nodes.desc: Recorded pedigree made a beast's line a priced good (memory): the book was the instrument.

nodes.label: Sugar beet progeny selection
nodes.desc: Mothers chosen by their offspring's sugar content raised beet sugar from roughly 6 to 7% to well over 12% (memory, rough), feeding Europe's beet sugar against cane.

nodes.label: Mendelian plant breeding
nodes.desc: Mendel (1866), rediscovered 1900, gave breeders a theory: rust-resistant wheats, then hybrid maize and the Green Revolution wheats (memory).

nodes.label: Industrial Enlightenment
nodes.desc: Mokyr: propositional knowledge widened along with techniques, and access costs fell through print, societies, lectures and journals (about 1700 to 1850). Contested by Allen (incentives) and by evidence that many inventions owed little to science.

nodes.label: Museum of Alexandria
nodes.desc: Royal patronage of scholars on stipends: Euclid, Eratosthenes, Ctesibius, Hero (memory). Prestige science with engineers and astronomers attached to a court.

nodes.label: House of Wisdom
nodes.desc: Abbasid translation of Greek, Persian and Indian works and astronomy for calendar and prayer times (memory).

nodes.label: Princely observatories
nodes.desc: Rulers and waqf endowments funded instruments and observers: al-Tusi at Maragha, Ulugh Beg, Tycho Brahe (memory). Patronage as a courtly gift economy (Biagioli).

nodes.label: Monastic learning and works
nodes.desc: Copying, literacy, estate improvement, water power and ironworks; the canonical hours may have driven the first mechanical clocks (memory). Long-lived holders of records and craft (part 16).

nodes.label: Medieval university
nodes.place: Bologna; Paris and Oxford by about 1200
nodes.desc: Law, medicine, theology and arts; about 60 to 80 in Europe by 1500 (rough, memory). A pool of the literate for church and state; crafts stayed outside.

nodes.label: Research university and teaching lab
nodes.desc: Teaching laboratories trained chemists by the hundred and joined research to teaching (memory); they supplied the dye firms' PhDs (part 08).

nodes.label: Scientific academies
nodes.desc: Societies of natural philosophers; the French academy paid members and advised the state on inventions (memory).

nodes.label: Scientific journals
nodes.desc: Journal des scavans and Philosophical Transactions (1665) made the dated printed report the unit of credit (memory); built on correspondence networks and the post.

nodes.label: Inducement prizes
nodes.desc: Rewards for set problems: Society of Arts premiums, the Academie's soda prize (1775), Appert's 12,000 francs (1810) (memory). Suited to known targets, as patents suit unknown ones.

nodes.label: Examined US patents and a patent market
nodes.desc: Cheap examined patents; Lamoreaux and Sokoloff found an active trade in patent rights through agents and lawyers (memory). Invention became a specialised trade.

nodes.label: Collective invention
nodes.desc: Engineers shared performance data after Watt's patent lapsed (part 07) and ironmasters shared furnace designs (Allen 1983, memory): improvement without patents.

nodes.label: Edison's invention factory
nodes.desc: Machinists, glassblowers, chemists and a library aiming at a minor invention every ten days (memory); produced the electric lighting system. Invention sold as a service.

nodes.label: Wartime science contracts (OSRD)
nodes.desc: Bush's office contracted universities and firms for radar, the proximity fuze and penicillin scale-up (memory).

nodes.label: Manhattan Project
nodes.desc: About 2.2 billion dollars and about 130,000 people at peak (June 1944); over 90% of the cost went to plants (checked). An industrial programme on a few years of physics.

nodes.label: Public science funding agencies
nodes.desc: After Science, the Endless Frontier (1945): grants for basic research; ARPA funded ARPANET and early computing (memory).

nodes.label: ARPA (DARPA)
nodes.desc: Founded after Sputnik (memory); funded the ARPANET (1969) and much early computing; defence buying took the first integrated circuits.

nodes.label: Soviet science cities
nodes.desc: Academy institutes apart from production; enterprises had weak reasons to adopt innovations (Berliner, memory). Strong science, weak diffusion.

nodes.label: R&D as a sector
nodes.desc: World R&D over 2.75 trillion dollars in 2023, nearly 2% of world GDP (checked); business did 74% of OECD R&D (checked); Israel 6.3% and Korea 5.0% of GDP.

nodes.label: Venture capital
nodes.desc: Finance for firms whose main asset is know-how (ARD 1946, memory).
